speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you have grouped Motions Nos. 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10 and 11 for debate. These are on a number of clauses which basically deal with the same subject.
Customs Tariff
We have expressed our concern about the way the Government has been dealing with the whole issue of its trade deal with the Americans.
Presently, the House of Commons committee studying this question is hearing witnesses from all across the country without having the final text before it. We are in a situation where the promise made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) in the House on October 5 has been ignored by the Government. At page 9632 of Hansard, the Prime Minister stated:
Mr. Speaker, I shall table the complete text of the Agreement as soon as the
wording is finalized. It will then be referred to the appropriate committee of
the House for analysis, study and debate.
On October 5, the Prime Minister promised the House and the people of Canada that the House of Commons committee would have the finalized document before the committee hearings in order that the committee could hear from witnesses from all parts of the country who had the document in front of them before he rushed off to Washington to sign the final trade deal.
It is now December 3, two months after the Government signed the Elements of Agreement, and we still do not have a finalized copy. Negotiations may or may not be taking place today to try to get a final copy of that document ready. It is now less than a month before the Prime Minister wants to sign a document which not one of us in the House has seen. This document is not even ready. Yet we know that it is a document which will fundamentally change the economy of this nation.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext: Improve.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Some say it will improve, some say otherwise. But the problem is that we do not have the document. There is presently a committee of the House in Halifax, and it does not have the document. There are witnesses appearing before that committee, and they do not have the document. It is not acceptable for us in the House to pass any legislation at this time which gives the Government a blank cheque when it comes to trade deals and tariff reductions. We will do nothing to make it possible for the Government through Order in Council to do what it should be doing through proper legislation, debate, our committee system, and through the House itself.
As I stated in an earlier speech, we will not expedite the passage of Bill C-87 because it helps the Government move along the road to its trade deal. We do not believe that, in any sense, passing legislation in a legitimate and orderly process is happening at this time.
If the Government was able to negotiate a deal with the Americans, as it claims it has done, all that had to be done was the following, to use the Prime Minister's words when he stated:

December 3, 1987
Customs Tariff
I am advised that there may be a minor typographical error in this document, but that the document itself represents the fundamentals of the agreement arrived at by the parties.
These elements are the agreed basis for the agreement and will be translated into a legal document, as agreed, in appropriate time frames by the negotiating teams.
The trade negotiators met late into last night and it is obvious that they failed to come to some finalized wording, and we are not talking about "minor" amendments. We are talking about negotiations which are ongoing and which could fundamentally alter the Elements of Agreement that we were shown two months ago. Obviously, the people of this country are very concerned about the agreement, regardless of whether they are for or against it. The Government has boasted how important it is. The people recognize it is important and we need a process, not a three, four, or five day debate prior to the Christmas recess, which the Government wants, a debate where the people of Canada will be excluded because they will not have seen the document, a debate which will occur after the committee has held hearings but without a final document in front of it.
When minor pieces of legislation are passed through the House of Commons, there is first reading one day, second reading later, a debate in the House, and then the Bill goes to committee. A finalized version of that Bill goes to committee, even if it is a minor piece of legislation. Witnesses are allowed to appear, pro and con, and then amendments can take place.
The Bill comes back to the House of Commons, as does this legislation that we are dealing with today, with other amendments being possible at report stage, as we call it. Following that there is third reading. Even for minor pieces of legislation, we are in the situation where the public has a final document, and they have the time to appear in front of a committee. In some cases even what we may call minor pieces of legislation have more witnesses appearing in front of a committee than is happening in the case of the trade deal.
I repeat, at least the witnesses who appear have a final document in front of them. The House of Commons at report stage, and later at third reading, is in a position to debate the merits of the legislation and to try to make amendments to it. Quite often ordinary legislation, some of it minor, some more important, takes a long time to get through the House of Commons. It is very seldom that we circumvent that route.
When it comes to the trade deal, the House of Commons cannot allow the Prime Minister to break his promise that we would have the finalized document and that that document would then go to the committee for study. The Prime Minister made a promise on October 5 and during later speeches he implied that it would be fulfilled some time during the month of October and there would be a final document. Therefore, when the committee travelled that final document would be in front of it.
October passed and we did not have a finalized document. November passed and we did not have a finalized document. It
is December and still there is no finalized document. Obviously, the committee which is scheduled to finish its work next Monday, will never have a finalized document in front of it. How can the Government, as it is doing at the present time, say that there will be a few days' debate just before the Christmas break, and it wants then to allow a vote on free trade so that our Prime Minister can go running off to Washington and say that he has the consent of the House of Commons? We do not do that for minor legislation. We certainly do not do it for major legislation. We will certainly not do it for the Prime Minister's trade package. The people of Canada deserve to have the information in front of them.

We are concerned about the manipulation of those different rates, which could take place without any public understanding or recourse to this Parliament, to determine whether a change is in the public interest.
The harmonization of rates that were agreed to under the previous GATT round, to which this Bill is giving implementation, is based on what I think is a crucial, fundamental principle of Canadian trade policy, that is, the application of non-discriminatory tariffs to all countries, and one of the unfortunate and debilitating effects of the proposed agreement with the Americans will be to set out discriminatory trade tariff rates that will work against that basic principle. Therefore, we would put ourselves in danger, I believe, of not only undermining our own trade relations with other countries who all of a sudden will wake up to find that countries which have been good customers of Canada are now treated to a discriminatory set of tariffs and that the Americans will get preferential treatment to the Japanese, the Russians or the Europeans.
This Parliament itself has not had the opportunity to comment on that to determine whether that version of trade may be a serious danger. Aside from our own specific trade relationships, I believe this dichotomy that we now have presents an erosion of the international trade system.
I would cite for Your Honour the statements made just last Sunday night by Paul Volcker, probably one of the most highly respected financial analysts in the world and head of the U.S. Federal Reserve Bank for close to eight years. He said very clearly that the emergence of regional trading blocs in North America, Europe and other places will undermine the international trading system through discriminatory trading practices.
That is the contradiction in this Bill when compared to the free trade agreement. You are saying to one class of customer that they will get preferential treatment. If that happens we will be back to where we were in the 1930s. Rather than having individual countries raise tariff barriers or treating one country differently from the other, we will now be doing it on a regional basis. We have brought the jungle-like atmosphere of the 1930s into the 1980s and 1990s and with the same effect, that is, trade wars on an international level between regional trading blocs.
The problem we have in this Parliament is that it is hard to get at the issue, which is what I was saying earlier. How can we raise these kinds of problems when we are subjected to a flying circus approach to the whole deal? We do not have an agreement, but we have a committee going through a farcical

Mr. Speaker, the basic purpose of this Bill is to establish a new harmonized system of tariffs between major trading nations, including Canada. There is no country for whom the question of tariffs and their effect on trade is more important than Canada. To a large extent we live by our ability to trade. Unfortunately, in recent years we have been faced by large groups of countries that are using tariffs and non-tariff methods to improve trade between themselves and restrict trade with other countries.
The European Economic Community has been extremely effective at removing tariffs between countries that belong to the community, and making it more and more difficult for other countries, including Canada, to sell to that community. The U.S. has followed a similar policy. Japan, that country to which we are urged to look as an example of how a free enterprise economy operates, has the most efficient and effective system of tariff and non-tariff barriers in the world. These include impossible standards which have to be met before one can sell to Japan. This has created tremendous difficulties for us.
A whole new set of difficulties will be created when this so-called free trade agreement with the U.S. is finally signed and put into effect. In the period before the 1984 election, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and his Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) derided the possibility of a free trade agreement with the U.S. On one occasion I think the Prime Minister compared it to an elephant dealing with a rabbit. That was the relative strength and power of the two countries as the Prime Minister saw it at that time.
During the election campaign, there was not a single mention of the possibility of a free trade agreement with the U.S. Then, because the Government saw that for more than a year it had been down at the bottom in support, based on polls done by Gallup, Angus Reid and The Globe and Mail, and looking for an issue which might bring it back, suddenly it brought forward the concept of a free trade agreement.

Mr. Speaker, the Chair has wisely chosen to group several motions for debate. I wish to address the principles of these motions today. I hope to be able to address as many of the motions which are before us as possible.
They all reflect a continuation of the struggle which began between the people and the monarchy as long ago as 1215 when King John was forced by the Lords of the day, who acted on behalf of the people, to sign the Magna Carta, which gave the very basic right for which we are fighting today with these amendments, that being the basic right of the Parliament of the country to establish what the rules should be with regard to the collection of taxes, the collection of government funds.
Under this particular Bill, approximately $2 billion worth of government revenues is at stake. The Government is proposing to do away with that revenue. Canada spends in the neighbourhood of $110 billion to $130 billion per year and has incurred a deficit in each year for the past three years in the neighbourhood of $30 billion. We are, therefore, not in a position to be giving away $2 billion worth of revenue.
December 3, 1987

Even more at issue is the fact that under Bill C-87 the power to reduce the amount of funds coming into the government Treasury by way of customs tariffs and other such revenues is being left essentially with the modern-day representative of the monarch, the Prime Minister and his Cabinet. We are seeing the age-old attempt under a constitutional monarchy by representatives of the Crown to make decisions with regard to the collection and expenditure of taxation without reference to the House of Commons which, under our system, is supposed to represent the people.
The principle which we are trying to establish with this series of motions is that within 60 days of the signing of an agreement which changes the procedure for the collection of tariffs, that agreement shall be submitted to the House of Commons for ratification. One would not think that this is a terribly radical initiative until you see the horror with which Members on the government side react.
We are attempting to continue a practice which was set in motion in 1215 and has been slowly and painfully continued through the centuries since then of putting the power to impose and collect taxation back into the hands of the House of Commons, which is the true representative of the people, rather than leaving it in the hands of the representatives of the monarch, namely the Prime Minister and his Cabinet.
We are not in any way restricting the monarch and her representatives, the Prime Minister and Cabinet, from undertaking initiatives by way of international treaties or by proposing changes to the amount of taxation which they will be levelling at or within our borders. We are simply asking for the maintenance of the ancient right that once decisions are made they cannot continue after 60 days without the approval of the House of Commons. This is not even as strong in some ways as that which the Lords demanded at Runnymede. We are saying "within 60 days" which seems to me to be a very reasonable request.
Two or three of these motions already in the first draft of the Act indicate that the Government is prepared to do so, would deign to do so, after 180 days. We are simply saying that we should speed up that process. This is consistent with some of the proposals made by both the McGrath commission and the Cooper commission, if I could call it that, two parliamentary groups which studied the activities of the House of Commons. The McGrath committee made proposals to strengthen the power of the back-benchers and of the Commons itself. The committee under the chairmanship of our friend, the Hon. Member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper), dealt with the question of parliamentary oversight and how Parliament could continue to build control over the budget and expenditure systems of this Chamber.
These proposed amendments which we are now discussing would force the Government to present such changes to our tariff laws, the amount of tariffs being levied at our borders,

within 60 days for approval by the House. This follows through with the initiatives the committee, chaired by the Hon. Member for Peace River, was attempting to impose on our processes in this Chamber. We were attempting to make the budgetary process more reasonable, to have the Chamber itself deal with government Bills. We were attempting to force the Government to come forward with government Bills in fact very closely in concert with the presentation of the Budget so that we could avoid the spectacle we often go through in this Chamber of imposing taxes, collecting taxes, income taxes and other taxes, long before the law actually passes this Chamber.
What we are trying to do from now on is to keep our procedures a little more tight and a little more proper in the administrative sense so that this Chamber does get a chance to do its job of overviewing the expenditure plans of the administration of the executive branch of the Cabinet itself. This Bill proposes to give away close $2 billion in Government revenues, and because the Government is already in a deficit position of around $30 billion per year, this money will have to be made up through the tax system by some other means. We think that because there are a host of possibilities before us at the moment with the clauses mentioned in this Bill. There are potential changes to the tariff rates with Great Britain, the United States and various Commonwealth countries, some of the nations which have already been granted most-favourednation status, and a great long list of others who may in fact be granted such status to the point where they may eventually pay zero tariff from the current high level of 35 per cent tariff.
We think that before the Government makes permanent such arrangements by treaty, which it has under our constitutional monarchy every right to do, that treaty or those obligations should be transferred in front of this Chamber within 60 days so that this Chamber could have the opportunity to reject or ratify them. We presume that in virtually all cases the Government will be a majority Government which will be assured of its taxing proposal, or its proposal to give away tax revenue. But the principle should remain constant. This Chamber, and this Chamber alone, should make the final decision as to whether or not that should be ratified. That is what these amendments are attempting to do. I would urge all Members of the House, whether in government or in opposition, to see the extreme importance to this Chamber and to the representative system in this country for that to be strengthened and to continue.

It is not the actions that are being dealt with here, it is the question of the accountability to Parliament. Clause 32 already requires approval by Parliament within 180 days. In other words, the principle of parliamentary accountability is there with respect to changes in the tariffs under Clauses 23, 27, and 28 of the Bill.
That means that if Canada extends or withdraws a most favoured nation tariff to another country for any or all goods-that is covered in Clause 23-that that must now be submitted for approval by Parliament by resolution within 180 days, or it lapses. It means that if Canada extends or withdraws a British preferential tariff to another country for any or for all goods, the Government must get approval from Parliament within 180 days, or else it lapses. It means that if Canada gives to any country that is presently under the British preferential tariff a more favourable treatment-that would be a less developing country, probably in Africa-then there too that is subject to parliamentary approval within 180 days. The principle of accountability to Parliament is an important one. The question referred to in my amendments in Motion Nos. 4 and 12 is simply whether the approval should come within 180 days or within 60 days.
I would argue that, on the basis of what we know about the Government's lack of trustworthiness and its lack of credibility in terms of making promises to Parliament, and through Parliament to the Canadian people, it is incumbent upon us to review the question of whether 180 days is an adequate time, or whether Parliament should not be called upon to act sooner, in other words, in these particular and important clauses and actions, whether the accountability to Parliament should not be tightened up and reaffirmed.

Therefore, I would judge that if we decided, for example, to give most favoured nation treatment to Albania, which I believe is now under the general tariffs, or withdraw MFN status from some other country because of a trade dispute, 1 do not imagine that if it were a routine matter it would take any parliamentary time at all. The experience in the recent past would indicate that my contention is an accurate one. The problem is that we now have the Government seeking powers in this Bill which would allow it to enter into a fundamental change, a Bill or agreement which would wreak fundamental change in our trading relationship with our largest trading partner. And through the back door, by means of this Bill, whose primary purpose is the harmonized system of tariffs, it is seeking to confirm for itself powers to do this without reference to Parliament. The Government's behaviour is reprehensible, and I believe it should be put on a short leash until it can demonstrate once again that it is worthy of the trust of the Canadian people, and it has some credibility in this particular area.
I heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) state in the House yesterday that no negotiations are taking place. But then on television I saw Mr. Murphy-Mr. Reisman went away by the garbage elevator-obviously rather emotional, upset and teed off at the situation, having come away from something which can only be described as a very tense and difficult set of negotiations.
We don't know whether they were negotiating the entire Auto Pact back, or down the drain, or whether they were negotiating in perpetuity that Canadian ship owners and sailors will never be able to serve American ports because of a perpetuation of the powers of the present Jones Act. The analogy is not perfect, because there is no power for the committees to actually confirm or refuse to confirm those appointments. Nonetheless, those appointments are referred to the relevant committee, and they lie on the table in that committee for a period of some three or four weeks or some shorter period, and the committees have the power, and I think it is accepted that the majority will not be used to stop that, actually to consider those appointments and whether or not they are appropriate.

Mr. Speaker, I support the position taken by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy). As he indicated, and as I said a while ago, we are not dealing with a normal situation. We are not dealing with a time when these changes in tariffs were fairly routine or when a great deal of discretion was left to the Government to change the schedules by Order in Council with little discussion in Parliament. It is our contention that the free trade agreement between Canada and the United States has changed the situation in a very fundamental way. For a few moments I will continue with the points I was trying to make with regard to how that changes the situation for Canadian farmers.
When Mr. Reisman said that agriculture was not affected because supply management and marketing boards were not mentioned, I meant it when I said that in my view and in the view of many farmers he was, to say the least, not telling the whole story. He was, to say the least, shading the truth. While supply management and marketing boards are not mentioned, the fact is that another part of the agreement removes the tariffs which Canada has traditionally put on processed foods.
Our chicken, turkey, egg, and other dairy producers operate under a supply management system through marketing boards. They are guaranteed, in return for agreeing to produce within a quota system, a price for their products which permits them to continue. It gives them the ability to continue. American producers do not have that system. Because American producers of chicken, turkey, and eggs have better weather, a larger market, subsidies for grain, and so on, they can sell their product cheaper than can Canadian producers. Their chickens, turkeys, and eggs can be processed into TV dinners, chicken pot pies, and chicken fingers for shipment to Canada and sold at a cheaper price than Canadian products.
I have checked that assertion or claim with leaders of the marketing boards in Manitoba and with the leaders of Keystone Agriculture, who are very cautious, conservative, good business types. I have also checked it with senior economists in the University of Manitoba Faculty of Agriculture. They agree with my description of how the system will work after the free trade agreement is signed. I would willingly defer to the Parliamentary Secretary, but since I am being invited to speak to this amendment I will gladly do so. This is an amendment to clause 32 of an Act respecting the imposition of duties of customs and other charges, to give effect to the International Convention on the Harmonized Commodity System, and so forth. I will spare you the long title of the Bill.
Mr. Speaker, clause 22 has to do with the accountability of the Government or the public administration and Parliament. This clause relates particularly to the ratification of any resolution or any decision under which certain imported goods would be subject to duties.

The purpose of the amendment, if I understand it properly, is to cut from 180 days, which is I think the present situation, to 60 days the time government orders relative to tariffs can have effect before they require ratification by a resolution of Parliament. These deal with accountability. It does not deal- and I agree with the Parliamentary Secretary-with anything to do with the present Canada-U.S. relations in regard to free trade or the so-called Mulroney-Reagan trade deal. It does deal with accountability. That is why I stand up, because 1 think over the years I have made the point that we should receive from Governments, on a regular basis, accountable reports as to how Ministers run the country.

Under the proposed amendment, Mr. Speaker, the Government would have only 60 instead of 180 days, and we suggest this would make for stricter control, better accountability, greater participation of the House in the administration of the country, and would provide Hon. Members with an opportunity to become familiar with a very complicated process.

Clause 23 allows the Government to extend or withdraw what was called most-favoured-nation tariffs. These tariffs are applied to any goods that originate in a country to which the general tariff applies. Normally it is set at about 35 per cent, which is a pretty high tariff. It applies to few countries that do not have essentially a very important trading relationship with Canada. The 35 per cent rate of tariff is so punitive that very few goods can get into Canada. Therefore, in order to gain access, these countries must negotiate for most-favoured-nations status for the goods they wish to sell in Canada or, alternatively, give Canada some reciprocal concessions. Hence this section does not deal strictly with the Canada-U.S. free trade negotiations. Nonetheless it permits the principle of parliamentary accountability to be argued.
I believe strongly that this is a well intentioned amendment. It is one that I think is done in the spirit of trying to get the Government to be more responsive to Parliament. I think it is what one might call a friendly amendment in trying to get parliamentarians more interested and, possibly through them, the public more involved in deciding what will happen with our tariffs and how we exclude or allow certain goods to be imported into this country.

Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government has called the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) trade deal a panacea for our fishing industry. The facts tell a different story. ALBERTA WILDERNESS ASSOCIATION-CONCERN FOR KANANASKIS MOOSE AND ELK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Alberta Wilderness Association has launched a court action against the Alberta Government to stop it from keeping open this winter a section of Highway 40 south of Mount Allan. Highway 40 runs through the Highwood Pass, a wintering area for elk and moose, and has always been closed to traffic after December 1. According to Diane Pachal, Executive Director of the AWA, there are no other areas for the moose and elk to go because a substantial area of wilderness habitat has been lost through development of Kananaskis country. The traffic will scare the elk and moose away, and in addition the highway could provide access for poachers.
Wildlife should not be put at risk because of the Olympics. We urge the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) and the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mr. Jelinek) to intervene and direct the Olympic Transportation Group to develop a traffic plan that will not require keeping Highway 40 open this winter through the Highwood Pass area. This is the least that must be done to protect the moose and elk of the Kananaskis.

Mr. Speaker, we are now dealing with the third grouping of proposed amendments to Bill C-87, which we were discussing earlier today. The point at issue in these amendments is that of time, and the role the Parliament of Canada should be playing with respect to changes to customs and tariffs agreements made between our country and others.
While dealing with previous groupings of amendments this morning, we discussed why it is so important, indeed vital, that the House of Commons be involved in the decisions made by
Customs Tariff
the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and his Cabinet concerning tariffs. I pointed out that this Bill covers some $2 billion worth of tariffs. I will not go over the implications of that again, but the two clauses to which we propose amendments today refer to the government proposal that those decisions it might make on an interim or ad hoc basis must come before this House within 180 days of their being made. To some people that may sound reasonable enough. It appears to be only about six months. That would give plenty of time, one would think, for the House to debate it, think about it, and deal with it properly.
However, I remind you and the House in general, Mr. Speaker, that when we talk about 180 days in Parliament, we are talking about 180 sitting days. This House seldom sits much over 180 days per year, so in this legislation we are granting authority to the Government to decide either to impose or to drop tariffs for virtually a year before this House will have a chance to look at it and decide whether or not it acceptable.
That runs completely counter to the principle that the House of Commons is the Chamber that makes decisions on whether or not people should be taxed, corporations should be taxed, or importers should be taxed on their goods sold in this country. This takes away the decision-making role of Parliament. It sets it aside for virtually one year, making it all but useless. Our amendment, which would change that 180 days to 60 days, is again being offered to both Clause 32 and Clause 61.
There are a couple of things I wish to say about Clause 61, but first I want to point out that there is a provision in Clause 32 which makes it clear that there will be times during the 60 days proposed that the House will not be able to sit because of an election and perhaps the Senate would be sitting during that time. I do not know why, but perhaps there will be some reason for the Senate to be sitting after the House has closed down before an election, and the sittings of that House are to be considered equally with our own in computing the 60 days we are proposing. Clause 32 says, among other things, that if something like that occurs and there is an election in progress, or the House cannot sit for some other reason, within 15 days after the resumption of that new Parliament a Bill would have to be presented and dealt with by the House of Commons. In that way the will of the people will be known on this particular item dealing with revenue and taxation.
Clause 61 has a slightly different slant to it. It deals with a period of time when the Governor in Council, which is the Cabinet, on a report of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) that Canada's external financial position and its balance of payments are such as to require special measures respecting Canadian imports, may, by Order, subject any goods that originate in any country or any class of those goods to a surcharge over and above the customs duties imposed pursuant to this Act. We are talking about a special circumstance, a near financial emergency, in which the Minister of Finance would suggest to the Cabinet that a special surcharge on the

import of a particular good or class of goods would be imposed.
It is my opinion that if the emergency is of that extent, it only makes sense for the House to be apprised of it and have dealt with it within 60 sitting days after the so-called emergency is brought forward. It is very critical for the role of the House of Commons that it be the place where decisions to impose extra charges are made. As I have pointed out, this has been fought for almost 800 years.
It is very difficult for us to know for how long we should continue to fight on this issue. Due to the grouping of motions and the decision to delay votes until all motions have been dealt with, we have had no response from government Members on where they stand on these particular proposals. We can, therefore, only continue to put the argument forward on each amendment because we have no idea whether our words are having any effect and whether the amendments will be accepted by the government side. As a consequence, I somewhat regret having to take this time to reiterate the point since we have not yet had a clear indication of what the backbenchers who are currently resident on the government side think about this issue.
All Members come to the House of Commons to represent their constituents and to be their voice in taxation matters. This particular Bill deals with the raising of revenue by way of import taxes, levies and duties. The proposal before us today would, in effect, do away with as much as $2 billion of revenues. That is an extremely significant amount if the Government intends eventually to balance the budget. Deficits have been running in the neighbourhood of $30 billion to $35 billion per annum. Therefore, we cannot easily throw away $2 billion without thorough consideration. This issue deserves the immediate response of the House of Commons.
We do not think that 60 sitting days puts undue pressure on the government of the day, whatever the era in which it may affect the Government. It is consistent with the principle of the report of the Member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper) who earlier recommended the swift passage of government financial Bills in order that back-benchers can have a proper and clear role to play in this Chamber. We therefore recommend to government Members these amendments in which we are proposing the reduction from 180 days to 60 sitting days of the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, we are presently debating Bill C-87, an Act respecting a harmonized tariff system and, in particular, Motions Nos. 4 and 12. Our concern with this Act is much greater under the circumstances surrounding the Mulroney-Reagan trade agreement than it would ordinarily have been. Ordinarily this type of Bill, which is fairly technical and routine, would be dealt with in a superficial manner in that it suggests that we are getting ourselves into line with all the other countries of the world in
the harmonized coding system for trade. However, the Bill becomes much more important under the Mulroney-Reagan trade deal because it will have a much greater impact than it would under ordinary circumstances. It therefore requires much closer scrutiny than would ordinarily have been given it.
As a result of the trade agreement certain tariffs will be put into effect almost immediately upon the signing of the agreement. Things which were routine in the past must now be questioned as a result of that agreement. Motions Nos. 4 and 12 are aimed at greater accountability of the Cabinet to Parliament. At present the Government can impose a tariff and ask for ratification of it by Parliament 180 days later. The barons faced King John because they wanted to go before the King more than once every two or three years to hear how much money he needed and what he needed it for.
The Government can now impose a tax on the people of Canada and need only ask Parliament for permission to do so more than a year later. The recommended changes in Clauses 32 and 61 would increase the responsibility of Cabinet to Parliament. Rather than being able to impose taxes and collect them for a year before having them ratified by Parliament, these amendments suggest that we reduce that time period to 60 days.
The Mulroney-Reagan trade agreement has brought the need for the accountability of the Cabinet to Parliament to the forefront. At present such an agreement can be signed by the Prime Minister, and the Government can bring forward a Ways and Means motion to impose or remove tariffs. That decision to impose or remove such tariffs will remain in effect for an entire year and, quite often, more than a year.
Our present year is 177 days. This Bill, at present, allows 180 days to be used up before the Government must come back to Parliament and have it ratified. Therefore, more than a year, at least 15 days into the next year, will be required before it is necessary to pass it. It seems wrong, in the view of democrats all over the world, to have a treaty signed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the President of the United States, to be put in place and negotiated by people who are not Members of Parliament, nor representatives of the people, a treaty which will abrogate the laws not only of the Parliament of Canada, because those tariffs were put in place by the Parliament of Canada, but also the laws of the legislatures of the provinces.
This treaty about which we are talking, or any kind of treaty or any Ways and Means motion which changes taxes, customs and excise taxes, does so without compunction and can do so, leaving those changes in place for a whole year before they have to come to Parliament for ratification. A treaty does not have to be accountable to Parliament. It can take off a tariff
December 3, 1987

which was put in place by Parliament, and it can be established technically as the law of the land just by the Government presenting the House with a motion which says that this is the action it intends to take.
Sometimes this motion is not even in the form of a Ways and Means motion, but in the form of a little line in a statement by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) as to what he is going to do in the next year in his Budget. However, it has the effect of law before it is brought before the House and ratified.
The 180 days really means that the will of Parliament has been sidelined. If we establish that tariff in Parliament, it is the will of Parliament that it be there. If it is eliminated, it is eliminated for a whole year without the will of Parliament. The will of Parliament has been sidelined for a whole year. I suppose some people will say that is part of the sloppiness of Parliaments because they are democratic and take a long time, but the point we are attempting to make in this particular motion is that we do not think it is necessary to sideline these issues for 180 days. In fact, I have often wondered why Ways and Means motions were presented and then no action taken for such a long time. Perhaps it is the sloppiness of doing business in Parliaments, but it is not good democracy.
It makes one wonder if perhaps we should not take a good hard look at the process by which we make treaties part of the fibre of the country. A treaty is signed by the Prime Minister and it becomes part of the fibre of the country. It does not have to come before Parliament, as the Canada-U.S. free trade agreement does not have to come before Parliament, to be accepted. All that is required is for the Prime Minister to have it approved by his Cabinet, but Cabinet does not represent the will of the people. It might think it does because three years ago approximately 50 per cent of the people voted for this Government, but just before the Government was elected the Prime Minister said in a statement that he would never touch free trade. Perhaps we have to look at the structure under which treaties are carried into law by this Government.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to join in this debate on Bill C-87. I might be quite prepared to do what the Parliamentary Secretary has just suggested and stick to the issue here and not express the concern about the Canada-U.S. trade deal that so many of us feel. However, let me leave that item and turn to Motions Nos. 4 and 12.
We are dealing with a Bill to provide for the imposition of duties of customs and other charges, to give effect to the International Convention on the Harmonized Commodity Description and Coding System, and so on. We are debating a measure which will make changes in the way in which we operate our customs tariff system. We are proposing a change in the time limits with respect to two of these clauses, namely, that the time limit in both Clause 32 and Clause 61 should not be 180 days, as it is, but should be reduced to 60 days.
I listened with great interest to the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) and the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo). The argument my colleagues and I have been making is that this is a principle of parliamentary accountability. These motions address the importance of having Parliament, the ultimate court of this land, the representatives of the people gathered together to make the law of the land, presented with these changes, which have been negotiated by the executive of Government with other countries at a much earlier point than the Bill would allow. That argument is one that can be addressed from various perspectives. Some of my colleagues have argued from the perspective of our current concern about negotiations between Canada and the United States. One can equally make that argument in national, political, and historical terms and, for that matter, not just national historical terms but in terms of the history of Parliament of England, the Parliament of the Commonwealth and of the British Empire Dominions in times past.
My friend, the Hon. Member for Prince Albert, alluded to King John and that famous encounter with the Barons. He was a monarch whose fault may in fact have been efficiency, a desire to increase his power, even more than it was a matter of his tyranny. He was greeted by the Barons who demanded that his Government not be solely a Government of the executive, of the King and his advisers doing what they thought made sense, but to respect the powers of the people. Of course, given the status-ridden society that prevailed in England and other countries of feudal Europe at that time, the Barons saw

December 3, 1987
Customs Tariff
themselves as the people who counted. They wanted the King to respect their position rather than act in an autocratic or arbitrary way.
The principle they were enunciating for King John at that time has come to be recognized by historians as a very important development in the history of Parliament. The principle that began in the time of King John stands today. The parliamentary Government in which we take pride is one which is government in the name of the Crown which must act here in Parliament.
It is completely inaccurate, indeed inadequate, for politicians who are sworn in as Ministers of the Crown to believe that what they initiate with their Departments and officials is inevitably right because it makes sense to them. There can be absolutely no doubt in the history of parliamentary Government in Canada that the executive brings its decisions here to ask for parliamentary approval.
Proposals in the form of Bills do not become the law of the land until they have been debated through several stages, considered in committee, and given the kind of detailed examination as we are involved in with Bill C-87 at the moment. It is simply a reflection of the traditions of Parliament to suggest that the decisions of the executive should be closely examined by Parliament long before 180 days, in the case of these tariff changes.
Many senior members of the Government are exactly those persons who made these arguments when they were in opposition. They are very familiar with the traditions of Parliament. Tragically, when they become Ministers, they forget those traditions and their back-benchers simply parrot the same line. They leave us with the impression that what makes sense to them is God-given insight on which one must act. It is nothing of the sort. Those decisions must be brought here and approved by Parliament.
Of course, given the political reality of their majority, they know that if they choose to press ahead with their policies, they can bull them through. However, they should have regard for history, tradition, and the nature of our Constitution to recognize the wisdom of having parliamentary consideration of these matters as early as possible.
If Members opposite are going to object to these two motions, as the Parliamentary Secretary just suggested, it is to their shame that I remind them of a long-serving Liberal Prime Minister of this country who is known to have uttered the phrase "Parliament if necessary, but not necessarily Parliament". He was known to believe he could proceed on his own and, if he could avoid debate on foreign affairs and policy relating to other countries, he would do so. There was a lack of debate on these matters for a number of years.
In that respect, let me allude to yesterday's statement by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) who
presented a report on his journey to Central America last week. Our critic, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), in responding to that statement, thanked the Minister for having made this report and giving us an opportunity for some consideration in the House of this very important aspect of External Affairs in this area of the new world of the Western Hemisphere, particularly Central America, where the United States has been involved for many years. Such a gesture only underscores the importance of Parliament.
I express intense regret at the Parliamentary Secretary's suggestion that the Government plans to oppose these motions. It is not true to the traditions about which they spoke eloquently and vehemently, and with profound conviction and passion when in opposition. Unfortunately, when the Government receives such a large majority, all that is forgotten and it simply uses the weight of numbers to do what it believes makes sense. That is regrettable, and Canadians who watch this debate will join with me in expressing regret that a Government would become arrogant even in its first term and not bother with Parliament.
It believes that a period of 180 days, half a year or more, is a sensible proposition. We are suggesting that 60 days is a reasonable period for a motion to be presented and debated. We could deal with these Ways and Means motions with the sense of importance they actually have in the affairs of Canada and our relations with other countries.
I strongly support Motions Nos. 4 and 8 and call upon members of the Government to join with us in passing these amendments.

He said: Mr. Speaker, this set of amendments gets to the core of the problem we see in the sections of the Customs Act which have been brought into this new Bill relative to the harmonized system of tariffs.
Through you, Mr. Speaker, I thank the official Mr. Speaker for his flexibility in giving me the benefit of the doubt in this particular case. There are four amendments and each of them indicate that the power conferred in the relevant clause should not be abrogated by any treaty between the Government of Canada and the Government of another country except by an Act of Parliament.
Customs Tariff
I recognize the Speaker's concern about that amendment. However, the essence of the position that is being put forward here is quite simply that by treaty we should not have a situation where Canada abrogates or loses the power to take trade action through retaliation under Clauses 59, 60, and 61, which provide for a form of retaliation, for a surtax, or for a surcharge. We should not be in a position where that type of power is taken away by a treaty. Obviously I am not thinking of a treaty between Canada and Upper Volta. I am thinking of the treaty which is currently in negotiations, no matter what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) says, between Canada and the United States on a freer trade arrangement.
If I had to rewrite the amendments in Clause 62, I perhaps may have changed them a little, but but the essence there is that we should not see a situation where Canada basically takes action to cut tariffs with the United States without reference to Parliament by means of an Act of Parliament. This is because the particular treaty which is currently being negotiated is of such fundamental importance to our two countries.
I wish to draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the extraordinary powers that now exist in Clause 62 of the Bill, powers which have existed in the past under the Customs Tariff. It reads:
62. The Governor in Council may, on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance, by order,
(a)	reduce or remove customs duties on goods imported from any country by way of compensation for concessions granted by that country or any other country, subject to such conditions as may be specified in the order; and
(b)	extend the benefit of any order made pursuant to paragraph (a) to any country as may be required by Canada's international obligations, subject to such conditions as may be specified in the order.
Subsequent to this debate there was another amendment which stated that Clause 62 may not be used in reference to Canadian duties against the United States, in other words, to prohibit the Governor in Council from exercising this power.
In this particular case, the amendment is that the power shall not be abrogated by means of a treaty which Canada signs. People say that that is very hypothetical, and they have never heard of it happening. The fact is that Canada is now embarked on a trade negotiation in which major elements of our sovereignty and our ability to make future arrangements to protect, enhance, or develop our industries in our economy are being taken away by means of treaty. In other words, we will not be able to act independently in the future.
While this does not bear directly on Clause 62, for example, I cite the granting of national treatment to American service industries which we understand is a part of the free trade agreement. In future, how the devil can the Parliament of Canada act to develop the services industries, which account for 70 per cent of our economy, if we have signed away our right to do so by a solemn commitment between Canada and another nation and if in fact this country has essentially told the Americans that we will not legislate in that area except that we first abrogate the agreement? After many years, the

December 3, 1987
Customs Tariff
agreement will become increasingly solidified and increasingly hard to shake away, and it will increasingly dictate the way our industrial structure is created.
This is why we are looking for a change here to recognize that the Government has moved us into a new type of situation, a situation where in a major way treaties can affect Canadian powers. Treaties did so in the past, but on a multilateral basis and in a minor, phased and graduated way. I would contend they did so in a way which was generally acceptable to Canadians who welcomed a freer trading environment which has been created on a multilateral international basis between Canada and other great trading nations over the 30 years or 40 years since the war.
However, if we get into trade disputes with the United States in future, disputes where in the past we had the power to impose increases in duties, surtaxes, or surcharges under Clauses 59, 60, or 61, we will be in a situation where the right of Canada to retaliate will have been signed away. Instead, that right will adhere in this new disputes resolution process and nowhere else.
How we will use that is something that I am not sure about. It seems to me that we will lack the weapons, because we will have tied our hands behind our backs. I would contend that we are dealing with a country that is grossly and gravely irresponsible in its use of trade actions as a weapon to hit at other countries that are smaller or economically weaker than it.
Unfortunately, despite the long-standing friendship between Americans and Canadians, and between our two great countries which has gone on for 150 years, it is nonetheless true that American industry has learned in a very fine way how to harass imports from other countries, including imports from Canada, and that the American Government either condones or encourages those types of situations.
The behaviour of the Americans since October 3 and over the course of the free trade negotiations does not give me a great deal of optimism that they have changed their tune and manners in this particular regard.
What has happened is that the Americans have continued to do such things as selling subsidized wheat into major markets that were traditionally Canadian, and imposing countervailing duties, for example, the 85 per cent on the potash industry, and generally trying to make life difficult for Canadians who were doing business in the United States. The Americans seem to have a rule in these things which is, "heads we win, and tails you lose".
In a situation where Canada has a natural advantage, for example with a particular natural resource, the Americans turn around and say, "The Canadian Government is not charging enough economic rent in order to counteract the natural advantage Canada has in the North American market, therefore those industries are being subsidized", which is what
happened in softwood lumber, and, "We will put a countervailing duty against Canada". That was the type of position the Americans took in that particular case.
The United States has natural comparative advantages in terms of trade with Canada in many different areas. For example, in the worst months of our winter there is more sunshine and warmth in Florida than there is right across Canada, except perhaps in Victoria where I come from, Mr. Speaker, and where you and I may meet after we retire. You may go there first though, Mr. Speaker; I expect to be around here for a while.
The Americans have advantages in terms of the economies of scale for certain industries, such as main frame computers, large scale machine tools, and certain other high-tech equipment. We will never overcome that advantage completely because our industries are smaller than theirs. Our niche is to find ways to do smaller, custom-made production runs efficiently using automation and computerization. These are our potentials.
The Americans take the view that their natural advantages, be it climate or economy of scale, should be allowed but that our natural advantages should be ignored. They have been using harassment techniques against Canadian goods in a very consistent way.
I suggest that the reason for these amendments is that Canada should not have its hands tied. If we find that the Americans are acting in bad faith after we have been dragged into a trade deal by the Prime Minister and his Government, we should not be unable to fight back if the Americans keep a loaded gun under the table. That is why we feel that these motions should be supported.

Mr. Speaker, these four motions which actually contain one amendment applying to four different clauses would allow the Parliament of Canada to have some power over treaties signed between the Government of Canada and the Government of any other country. These amendments follow directly upon the amendments we have suggested to Clause 59.
The amendments provide that the powers conferred by the relevant sections may not be abrogated by any treaty between the Government of Canada and the Government of another country except by an Act of Parliament. That gives the Parliament of Canada, and consequently the people of Canada, a bit more security.
The Government of Canada has negotiated such treaties in the past. For example, about seven or eight years ago, Canada negotiated a treaty with the United States on the Grand Banks fisheries. When the treaty was signed and approved by Cabinet, it became law in Canada. However, the process it followed in the United States was somewhat different. The American administration signed it but when it got to Congress,
December 3, 1987

Congress turned it down. Consequently, the agreement which we had signed in good faith and thought was settled turned out not to be so.
There is no process in Canada allowing the Parliament of Canada to approve a treaty. If this were to be done on a blanket basis, it may to some extent require a constitutional change. However, in these four motions, we are suggesting that Parliament will have the power the U.S. Congress has as a matter of course in these particular areas. Consequently, these motions are worded almost identically and will amend Clauses 59, 60, 61, and 62 to provide the Parliament of Canada the power to decide whether or not a particular treaty signed by Cabinet affecting a particular product or tariff should be accepted.
This power becomes more important in light of the scenario established under the Mulroney-Reagan trade agreement. We must be concerned about how such treaties are put in place. There is now not only a great disparity between how Canada approves a treaty and how the United States approves a treaty but added to that is something which greatly affects the powers of treaties. In the free trade agreement, there is a dispute-settlement mechanism which allows U.S. law to be applied to Canadian products.
In the process of accepting this treaty or any future treaty, we will, because of the Mulroney-Reagan trade agreement-

speechtext: Order, please. The Hon. Member who has been here for a number of years realizes that he is not to use the Prime Minister's name. I have heard this phrase a number of times today. There is no such thing as a Mulroney-Reagan treaty; it is the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and Mr. Reagan.

I accept your admonition, Mr. Speaker.
The trade agreement puts in place a dispute settlement mechanism which allows U.S. law to apply to Canadian products that go to the United States. TTrade disputes on countervail and anti-dumping that have been initiated by American companies against Canadian exporters are decided under U.S. law, and the decision then affects Canadian exporters.
There has already been a good example of this in the exports of softwood to the United States. The Americans put a countervailing duty on softwood and we reacted by putting a tax on the softwood that was to be exported from Canada. Consequently, the citizens of both nations are now paying more to build their houses. This has occurred because U.S. law was applied to this trade question.
With these motions, we are attempting to ensure that Canada, through Parliament, can have a say when it finds that it is being wronged by U.S. law under the treaties signed by the executive branch of the United States and the Cabinet of Canada. The motions provide that we have some recourse, the
Customs Tariff
recourse being that the decisions made under U.S. law cannot affect Canadian decisions without passing through Parliament.
The motions would also give Parliament more of a democratic grasp on the establishment of the kind of country in which we want to live and the kind of relationships we want to have with other Governments. If the Government of Canada through a treaty gives up its power to establish tariffs-that is what happened in the past-then we have to have some way in which to limit that power. These amendments will attempt to do that.
Maybe what we need is to take a good look at the process of treaty establishment in Canada. Maybe we need to change the tradition and make all treaties referable to Parliament instead of the way it is now. When a decision is made for a treaty it is accepted as being complete when signed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and approved by Cabinet. If these amendments are put in place, we will at least have some of the treaties sent to Parliament or approved by Parliament at some stage before they become the law of Canada.
The trade agreement between the United States and Canada has been based on, or at least the rhetoric which the agreement is based on, the requirement for a level playing field. I suggest that a level playing field requires the same kind of approach to the ratifying of a treaty as we have for organizations and the law to be applied on both sides of the border. That has not been done.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the amendments of these five different motions that appear in different parts of the Bill which are trying to establish the same principle throughout the Bill. We have here as important a proposition as that in the Lord's decision to approach King John and force him to permit the Parliament of the day to approve any changes to the taxing and spending power of the Government. What we have here is an attempt in a constitutional monarchy to change the way that our Government conducts itself in international affairs with regard to the signing of international agreements and treaties.
What it says is very straightforward. The amendments we are proposing in the five places in the Bill where it is appropriate to move them very clearly say: "The powers conferred by this section may not be abrogated between the Government of Canada and the Government of another country''. This would make Parliament supreme in the functions of any Government, regardless of what stripe that Government might be. The Government would have to take changes to the treaty-in this case an abrogation of the treaty-back to the House of

December 3, 1987
Customs Tariff
Commons, the Parliament of Canada, before the Government could change or abandon the treaty.
This would be of interest to Members on the government side. Knowing past history they will realize that they will not be on the government side forever. If the Government changes, which the current status in the polls indicates as a foregone conclusion, one or the other of the opposition Parties will form the new Government. If we can believe the leaders of each of those Parties, they have every intention of abrogating this Canada-U.S. accord we have been discussing this afternoon.
Government Members would, I am sure, were they on our side of the House, be quite concerned that they have some say in a decision about the treaty. I presume they think the matter should be brought to the House of Commons by way of an Act of Parliament before any changes or a complete abrogation of the treaty were made. I presume we would get full support of government Members, particularly those who have been attempting to change the role of the back-bencher in the House of Commons. I see the Hon. Member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper) is in his place. I presume that he will be supporting this amendment because it increases and clarifies the role of the House of Commons and gives it a role in the finalization of treaty obligations that any Government may make on behalf of the country. This is extremely important. We have followed 800 years of British parliamentary practice, namely, whoever is the Government represents a majority of the people and, therefore, speaks for them. Because of that majority, it has every right to sign an international treaty.
However, we are at the point right at the moment, if I can divert from the Bill itself just to make an example, where the Government is proposing an international treaty with the United States, a Government that no longer has the backing of the majority of Canadians. In fact, if we can believe the opinion polls, about one Canadian voter in four supports the Government. The henchmen of the agreement, the Premiers, allegedly behind the Prime Minister's attempt to go forward with this agreement, are in similar disarray. The Premier of my province, Grant Devine, is reported to be running 25 points behind the NDP's Roy Romanow, but Grant Devine is one of the leading advocates of this particular agreement. He does not have a majority of support in his own province yet he is attempting to speak for the whole of the country, which is his right under our system. But he is not speaking for a majority and he is not representing a majority. In fact, his Government got 2,000 votes less than the Official Opposition. The Premier of British Columbia is currently running 11 points behind the NDP in that province and even that rock of Conservative solidarity in your own province, Mr. Speaker, of Alberta, is seeing Premier Don Getty falling in the polls as his support for this agreement is recognized.

speakerposition: Minister of the Environment
speechtext: What are the polls in Manitoba? Where does Howard Pawley stand?
He is not doing that particularly well.
Oh, oh!

He is at least equal to the Conservatives in his province. The rural areas in Manitoba, I might point out, in the last poll were up 6 per cent over the previous one. But there is some concern about what the Government is proposing to do with this country. I raise that point to reinforce the argument I am trying to make, namely, that it is important to refer back to Parliament before we rely wholly on the executive branch of any Government.
I do not care whether it is a Government our Party would form or one of the other Parties might form. The principle should be changed so that Parliament has the right to deal with international agreements of this nature. Whether it is an agreement to harmonize tariff rates, or to form an economic union with another country, Parliament should be consulted. It should be considered as a new principle of democratic Government that such agreements have to have the approval of Parliament before they come into place.
This is necessary because opinions change and the direction of Governments change. There is no clearer example of that than the current Government. During the leadership campaign of the government Party, we were told by the man who eventually became Leader that free trade with the U.S. was something he would hear no more of, that it could lead to a loss of sovereignty and so on. We also know that in November, 1984, shortly after becoming Prime Minister, that same gentleman said: "We have only been in power for two months but I can tell you this: Give us 20 years, and it is coming, and you will not recognize this country." A few years later, on October 22, 1987, just after the deal was signed with the Americans, Clayton Yeutter, U.S. trade representative, said: "The Canadians don't understand what they have signed. In 20 years they will be sucked into the U.S. economy." I wonder if the Prime Minister is not keeping one of his promises, the one he made on September 7, about giving him 20 years and we would not recognize this country.
That is one of the reasons I think Parliament has to have an opportunity to review trade agreements, international accords, and changes to tariff rates such as we have before us today. It is extremely vital to the continuation and modernization of the democratic process that these amendments be made.

It is one of those days, Mr. Speaker, but I am rising to speak particularly to Motion No. 8 put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy). It reads:
"(7) The powers conferred by this section may not be abrogated by any treaty between the Government of Canada and the government of another country except by an Act of Parliament."
This motion should be accepted, and I encourage the Government to do so. It is very similar to provincial planning laws and municipal zoning laws which establish a set of rules with respect to how a community is to be developed. If one wants to change those rules, one has to go through a public process. One just cannot sit in a community room or cabinet room or council room and redraw the lines and it is done. One has to go through a public process. What we are saying in this motion is that if this and other amendments are put in place, the Government would have to bring in a specific piece of legislation for a specific commodity or component in order for the tariff to be changed. What we are trying to do is maintain that opportunity in the public forum.
In general we are concerned that this Bill, and that clause in particular, will open the door for implementation of the trade agreement reached between the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) and the President of the United States. We want to prevent that. We want to put this clause in so that the normal ability of a Prime Minister to sign a treaty is taken away from him. If he wanted to do something like that, he would have to come back and change this particular Bill based on that agreement. We think it is very appropriate to put that kind of power in the legislation and ensure that the people of Canada, through their elected representatives, have the fullest opportunity to debate the impact of changes.
Customs Tariff
Yesterday I had the opportunity, along with my caucus colleagues, to meet with two individuals who were very concerned about one of the industries to be directly affected by the trade agreement. They were representatives of the Ontario Grape Growers Marketing Board. They explained to us the implications for grape producers in Ontario. Even though they did not represent them, the same holds true for grape growers in British Columbia. This would have a devastating impact on the business, their families, and their employees. They said the impact was not going to occur in 1989; it was going to be in 1988 because of the growing season in that industry. They will have to begin now to remove from production those vines that will be producing in 1989. Already they will have to down size their production.
They pointed out that whereas Canada was giving up its industry, particularly the wine industry which uses these grapes, they were not getting guaranteed access to the U.S. Americans can sell their wine and juices in Canada without any financial impediment. However, Canadian producers do not have the same access to the United States markets primarily due to the concentration of ownership in the distribution system. In most of the United States the distribution system is controlled by one of the biggest wine producers in the country. I believe that more than three-quarters of the States are controlled by that one company.
It is clear that Canadian wine producers have not had a fair shake. They have not had access to the market equal to that which American producers have been given in Canada. That is assuming that the provinces, particularly Ontario, will go along with the deal. Unfortunately it seems that the Province of Ontario, in spite of the strong show during the last provincial election about vetoing this deal if it is bad for Ontario, will not live up to its word. I think that in time the people of Ontario will realize that they were sold a bill of goods by the Liberal Party of Ontario.
The trade agreement is an extremely important matter for Canadians as well as for Americans. The Canadians to whom I have spoken, Canadians of all political stripes, have expressed real concern about what they perceive to be the implications of this agreement which allows our very large neighbour to the south to come in at will, with no protection for Canadians, to sell their products. In some cases we can sell our products in their market, but they do not see the balance.
Some people think it will be great to be able to go to the United States and pick up a VCR or a television set for $99.99. They do not realize that those things are not made in the United States. They are made elsewhere and would not be included in the agreement.
Granted, there will be a reduction in the price of some items which people will be able to purchase in the United States because they will be able to bring them back to Canada dutyfree. However, they will still have to pay provincial and federal

December 3, 1987
Customs Tariff
sales tax. They also forget that the merchants in their communities will no longer have the same volume of sales and will have to charge more per unit, in order to maintain their standard of living and ensure that the return on their investment is appropriate.
There are two implications of that. Thunder Bay is 190 miles from its major neighbours in the United States; Duluth, Minnesota, and Superior, Wisconsin. People will not be able to go there every week. But enough people will go there to cause a serious decline in the revenues of retailers in Thunder Bay. The times they are not able to go to the United States they will have to pay more at home. The people who do not have the ability to travel to Duluth or Grande Marais, which is a smaller community closer to Thunder Bay, will not benefit by that and will have to pay more. In addition, fewer small businesses will be able to survive in an already fragile situation.
Although the idea of free trade sounds great, as though we will be getting something for nothing, there is no such thing as something for nothing. When we study the details of the agreement we begin to understand that it is not such a great deal. That is why we have been demanding the right to see the details. We want to examine the nuts and bolts in order to determine what it means to commodity x, y, and z, what it means to British Columbia, Atlantic Canada, and northern Ontario. As a result of the softwood lumber deal northern Ontario was hit hardest. For that reason we believe that Motion No. 8 in particular should be accepted by the Government in order that it cannot automatically implement the trade deal.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to lend my support to the amendments proposed by my colleague. 1 do so because we believe in the principle that Parliament, through the majority of its Members, should have the right and ability to make decisions which are of importance to Canadians and will have very serious effects on them. That is why we moved this amendment.
In our view the Government, which has a large majority in this Parliament, did not get a mandate to negotiate a free trade deal with the United States. As I indicated in debate earlier today, and as my colleagues and others have frequently made clear, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) never at any time told the people of Canada that he believed that a free trade agreement with the United States would be beneficial to the people of Canada.
Indeed, in 1983 and 1984, before the election, the Prime Minister made very clear his rejection of the idea of free trade describing the relationship between Canada and the United States in very clear and very correct terms. He classified the United States as an elephant and Canada as a rabbit. I have to agree with him in terms of the relative strength of Canada and the United States as he described it then. During the election campaign he never dealt with the question of free trade at all.
We have estimated that the Prime Minister and his colleagues made over 200 promises during the course of that campaign. One would have thought that they had covered every possible aspect of Canadian life, but there was not one mention of free trade during the entire election campaign. Suddenly, as I said earlier, because of the low standing of the Conservative Party in the polls, the low standing which has continued for 16 to 18 months, the Government, looking for an issue which might gain it the support of the Canadian people, seized on this. One can accept the attraction of free trade, if there was a genuine agreement for free trade between these two countries. One could understand, although I happen to disagree with the recommendations of the Macdonald Commission of a free trade agreement between the United States and Canada. There is a world of difference between what the Macdonald Commission was recommending as a free trade agreement between Canada and the United States and what we have now, or at least what we know about what we have now, which is very little. It is like comparing night and day.
What we have here is an agreement which gives the advantages to the United States and all the drawbacks and disadvantages to Canada. We know from watching Mr. Reisman and the United States negotiator, Mr. Murphy, that the Americans are not satisfied with the fact that in the October agreement they took us to the cleaners. They now want another kick at the cat.
