I remind Members that just a few days before the agreement was signed in October, our negotiator, Mr. Reisman, picked up his hat, coat, and briefcase and walked out, saying no way was he going to agree to the demands the Americans were making. A few days later he was back and he did agree on behalf of the Government of Canada. Why did he agree? Because he received his marching orders from the Prime Minister.
Mr. Reisman is an able, experienced negotiator.
That is his job.

Of course, that is his job. That is how the democratic system works. Part of the democratic system that is not working in this present debate is that the people of Canada, Members of Parliament, and the provincial Governments are being asked to buy a pig in a poke. We are being asked to accept that the federal Conservative Government, which never talked about free trade, should now be able to sign an agreement, the final text of which will run into several thousand pages, without the agreement of Members of Parliament, the Premiers of the provinces, or various economic and cultural groups which have a vital interest in what the agreement will contain because they will be so enormously affected either for good or for evil. No one knows what is in the final agreement. No one knows what is involved in the 2 per cent over which they are still haggling and discussing.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order.

Mr. Speaker, I take it we are on Motions Nos. 8, 11 A, 12A, and 13A. I want to speak in support of those motions.
It has always been my view, if you do not mind, Sir, that the ratification of treaties and international agreements must in the present context, be carried on by the Government of the day-not just by the Prime Minister, Cabinet, or a combination of both-and ratified by the House of Commons and only the House of Commons.
Our amendments say that any treaty or portion thereof cannot abrogate any section of this Bill without the consent of Parliament. I admit right away that that may be a back door way of going about it. However, we are left with no other choice. What we are faced with is that in our parliamentary democracy we are permitting a foreign administration to tell a supine, money hungry Government of Canada what kind of laws we must have. We are dealing with a law that calls for the harmonization of tariffs and duties and so forth.
Customs Tariff
As I said the other day on an earlier amendment, the Government wants us all to get into harmony, and the name of the tune will be the Star Spangled Banner. Obviously our amendments to this Bill-and we have done the same on other occasions on other Bills, some of them long past-indicate that my Party would bring to Parliament any international agreement or treaty for debate, discussion, and ratification whether or not it required a constitutional amendment. I think it should be a requirement. If the House of Commons chose not to approve or ratify a treaty, be it a trade agreement or any other kind of international treaty, the Government of the day, particularly if it was a Government of my Party, would have to go back to the negotiating table of the country or countries concerned.
My friends opposite continue to suffer the delusion that the United States administration or Congress, or the individual 50 states, will hold still for Canada obtaining a larger share of any market in any commodity than we presently have. In my own part of Canada many suffer from the same delusion, specifically the Cattlemen's Association and some hog producers.
We have learned enough lessons from free trade arrangements in the past, when they closed down the border, countervailed, established duties or tariffs in spite of a non-tariff arrangement. As I read the agreement, there is nothing that prevents the United States from doing the exact same thing again.
While I will not say it is a sell-out, the Government is prepared to go to almost any length in a desperate effort to obtain a treaty. I received information this morning from a senior federal bureaucrat that the Americans have in fact thrown new flies in the ointment, and the negotiations on matters which we were assured by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) were completed are still going on.
We find it necessary to move these kinds of amendments because the Americans have thrown new wrinkles into the present discussions. We are in the dark about negotiations at the moment, and we have no other choice but to put forward these amendments which say these powers cannot be abrogated by any treaty or portion thereof.
This morning in the transport committee 1 tried to raise questions concerning the transportation annex. If and when the Government brings in legislation amending some of our transportation laws, it will have to answer some questions about the present agreement. Section 4 of the transportation annex speaks of the making of amendments to existing measures or future measures taken pursuant to existing measures, subject to the test of unfair subsidy. It was impossible to get an explanation from senior officials in the Department of Transport about what constitutes an unfair subsidy.
It states that new measures in areas not addressed by existing measures are subject to the test of an unfair subsidy.

December 3, 1987
Message from the Senate
How will an unfair subsidy on a transport rate or program be defined? They were unable or unwilling to tell us.
Is a government payment a necessary condition to define a subsidy? What if a transportation operation cross subsidizes among its traffic? Will an unfair subsidy be based on variable cost, short-run and long-run, constant cost, or fixed cost?
More important, if we were to index fully the western grain freight subsidy against inflation, would that be subject to the test of an unfair subsidy under the transportation annex to the free trade agreement? No one in the Government, including the Prime Minister, will respond to that question. That is another reason for these amendments.
Let us assume, for the benefit of my friends from Atlantic Canada, that we want to change the percentage of rate of subsidy on goods shipped out of the Atlantic region. Would the new subsidy be subject to the test of an unfair subsidy as laid down in the free trade agreement and the transportation annex? Could the rates consequently be affected?
Would the subsidized construction of a new rail line or air cargo terminal be subject to the test of an unfair subsidy? Could the rates be affected? These concerns are another reason for these amendments. Anything in this Bill could not be abrogated by the treaty the Government is presently negotiating, without coming to Parliament. Surely the Government would accept such a proposal if the deal is so good.
The U.S. Jones Act restricts domestic cargo to American vessels. Will there be an amendment to the trade deal to give us the same right, should we ever decide to use it?
